# OWASP GenAI Security Project, Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026, Warranting Agent-Built Software Distillation

**Source:** OWASP GenAI Security Project, *OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2026*, Version 2026, dated August 4th, 2026 on the cover; Project Lead Steve Wilson, Co-Lead Rock Lambros; genai.owasp.org. **Scope:** open. Citations take the form `(LLM0N, p. N)`, printed page numbers, with the risk ID where one applies.

**Licence and share-alike notice.** The source is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0 (p. 2). This distillation is an adaptation of it: the source's guidance condensed, paraphrased, reordered and projected onto the task of warranting agent-built software, with short verbatim quotations marked `[V]`. It is shared under the same licence, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/). Attribution: OWASP GenAI Security Project, genai.owasp.org. The source states it is not legal advice (p. 2), and nothing here adds to that.

**Setting, read before projecting.** The list owns the risk of a model working as a *component* inside an application; once the model acts, with tools, memory and downstream consequences, the source hands the risk to the OWASP Agentic Top 10 and tells readers to pair the two (p. 7). It reaches this axis by two routes. First, when a change adds a model feature (an LLM call, a prompt, a tool the model can call, retrieval or memory), the ten entries are the threat list for that feature, as written. Second, the coding agent itself is an LLM application with tools: the source's own scenarios include an IDE coding assistant whose repository took a destructive system prompt and which a runtime injection made run arbitrary code (LLM01 Scenario #8, p. 16), and developer assistants reading planted text in an issue, a ticket or a package under elevated credentials (Scenario #9, pp. 16–17); and it says Improper Output Handling now spans the insecure code assistants generate at scale (p. 7). Those items apply to the builder's harness directly. Where this distillation carries an application-feature control across to the coding agent's own sandbox, it marks the move as a transfer. The source is threat guidance, not a measured study of its controls; it states each control's limit, and this distillation keeps those limits.

**Applicability gate (Pass G.0): clear yes.** (1) The source answers questions this axis asks: what a change that adds a model, tool or memory touches and which gates that makes mandatory; what the worst irreversible thing the agent can do is, and what stops it; which claims are demonstrated and which only asserted (its Claim-Check-Act pattern and its scenario of fabricated task completion); and whether a quiet record is evidence of safety (its *defense effect*). (2) Its controls land on all eight phases, strongest on triaging model features, building in the sandbox and gating. Phase 1 gets only capability and output contracts for model features; nothing speaks to acceptance criteria for ordinary behaviour. Phase 6 gets review coverage, not reviewer independence. (3) Its contrarian positions (defense is architectural rather than interceptive; reject static-only attack claims; signing is not safety; alerts are not caps; authorization never in the model) bear directly on what a warranty pack may count as a control.

**Phase mapping.**

| Phase | Fit | What the source brings |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Specifying the change | Partial (model features) | A capability budget for the feature (which of untrusted input, sensitive data and state change or external communication it holds); minimal tools, functionality and permissions; which actions need a human; a strict output schema; a spend ceiling. Nothing on acceptance criteria or non-goals |
| 2 Triaging risk | Strong (model features) | Ten entries to route a feature by its shape; the three-leg check and the two-of-three floor; every disclosure channel treated as an output; authorization before retrieval; memory writes as privileged; hidden-context severity tiers; a graduated enforcement policy by reversibility |
| 3 Locking the tests | Moderate | Adaptive red-teaming over static attack sets; planted instructions per indirect surface; hostile payloads per output sink; checking state rather than claims; trigger-probing for backdoors; disclosure red-teaming as a release gate. Nothing on who writes the tests or tests edited to pass |
| 4 Building in the sandbox | Strong, direct for developer assistants | Indirect injection through trusted surfaces; credentials held in code, not the model; human confirmation of the exact rendered action; AI-suggested dependencies verified; tools and MCP servers pinned, signed and their descriptions audited; agentic circuit breakers; fabricated completion |
| 5 Gating deterministically | Strong | Output encoded or parameterized per sink; control characters and auto-render handled; invisible Unicode stripped; structural validation in trusted code; no secrets in hidden context; immutable digests; hard caps; scanners and safe formats as layers, not guarantees |
| 6 Reviewing independently | Partial | Review that covers indirect surfaces, where authorization lives, and each control's stated limit; LLM-generated code deployed without human review or security testing as a named scenario. Nothing on who reviews |
| 7 Warranting the change | Moderate | Two kinds of control (those that reduce injection success and those that bound the blast radius); residual-risk assessment for two-leg configurations; adaptive results only; signing proves origin, not safety; severity by what a recipient can learn |
| 8 Releasing and operating | Moderate | Hard caps, cost attribution and session-level cost growth; tool-use monitoring; observability platforms that capture prompts by default; a disclosure incident-response playbook; embedding leaks treated as source-document leaks |

Triggers addressed: 15 of the seed table's 41 (see the runtime section). No trigger-mismatch flag. Phases 5 and 6 match no seed trigger; their rows are logged as extensions.

## Warranting Agent-Built Software Relevance

The list gives an accountable builder one stance and a set of named controls for any change that puts a model inside the software or lets an agent act. The stance comes first, from the project leads: "Stop trying to build a model that cannot be fooled." [V] Instead, "Build the system around it, so that when the model is fooled, and it will be, nothing important breaks." [V] (p. 5). For prompt injection the source states the consequence plainly: it is "intrinsic to current generative AI" [V], "no reliable prevention mechanism exists today" [V], and so "Defense is therefore architectural rather than interceptive." [V] (LLM01, p. 13). For a warranty, that sorts the evidence. Some controls reduce the chance of a successful injection and are expected to degrade against adaptive attackers; others bound the blast radius once injection succeeds and survive attackers who can probe the system, and for agents the source calls least privilege and capability budgeting load-bearing (LLM01, p. 13) [AR]. A pack whose only injection control is of the first kind has not warranted the feature.

The same entries speak to the coding agent the builder runs. An agent that reads a public issue or a support ticket while holding the developer's credentials is the source's indirect-injection case: "The agent, not the attacker, performs the privileged action" [V] (LLM01, p. 12). An agent's report that it finished is the source's misinformation case, where "The core risk is that the incorrect output is trusted and acted upon." [V] (LLM07, p. 43), down to a scenario of an agent reporting a backup that never ran (LLM07, p. 45) [AE]. And a dependency the agent suggests may be a name an attacker registered because models hallucinate it (LLM04, p. 28) [BT]. The list's limits matter as much: it covers the model as a component and hands agentic amplification to the Agentic Top 10 (p. 7); it is a consensus product weighted three-quarters to a practitioner vote and a quarter to incident data (p. 5); and its controls are recommendations with stated limits, not measured effects.

## Key Concepts for Warranting Agent-Built Software

1. <!-- concept: build-for-the-fooled-model --> **Build for the day the model is fooled; a quiet record is a defense effect.** The leads' posture runs through all ten entries (p. 5) [AR]. Practitioners rank prompt injection first while the raw incident record drops it out of the top 10: "That gap is a defense effect." [V] Teams fight injection hard, so fewer clean exploits reach a public database, and the public count understates the risk mature teams spend money holding off (p. 5) [AR]. The closing instruction: "Work all ten, start at the top, and build each of them for the day the model is turned against you." [V] (p. 8). For this axis, a team's own quiet months read the same way (transfer): an absence of incidents is what the controls bought, not proof they can go.

2. <!-- concept: architectural-not-interceptive-defense --> **Two kinds of control, and adaptive testing.** Defense-in-depth, since no single control suffices: some controls reduce injection success and are expected to degrade against adaptive attackers; others bound the blast radius once injection succeeds and survive attackers who can probe the system; for agentic deployments, least privilege and capability budgeting are "load-bearing" [V] (LLM01, p. 13) [AR]. Each of the eleven LLM01 controls carries its stated limit (pp. 13–15) [AP]. Control #11: test against adaptive attackers who have read the deployed defense and reject static-only attack-success claims; a study the source cites "found static attack success near zero while adaptive attack success exceeded 90% for most of 12 recent defenses" [V] (LLM01, p. 15) [BT].

3. <!-- concept: indirect-injection-through-trusted-surfaces --> **Indirect injection, including through trusted surfaces.** Any input the model reads can carry instructions: retrieved content, tool output, images, audio, intermediate reasoning, persistent memory (LLM01, p. 10) [AP]. Models make no architectural distinction between instructions and data, so there is no clean equivalent of parameterized queries (p. 10) [BT]. Surfaces run from untrusted (public web, unknown-sender email) through semi-trusted (public issue titles, package READMEs and changelogs) to trusted (the developer's own repositories and databases, where an attacker may have placed content through an unrelated public form) (pp. 11–12) [AR]. "Defenses that focus only on the chat surface miss this entirely." [V] (p. 12). The attacker submits text through a low-privilege channel and waits for the user's MCP-connected agent or developer assistant to read it under elevated credentials (p. 12) [AR]. An injection can even happen with no malicious party, as when a job ad's hidden instruction meets an applicant's LLM-polished resume: "a prompt injection with neither party acting maliciously" [V] (Scenario #3, p. 15).

4. <!-- concept: capability-budget-three-legs --> **The capability budget: three legs, and the two-of-three floor.** The source restates the structural diagnosis as a pre-deployment check it cites from prior work: an agent that can at once reach private data, ingest untrusted content and communicate externally has the conditions for high-impact exploitation, and removing any one leg removes them (LLM01, p. 13) [BT]. Control #8 budgets capabilities with a two-of-three rule, also adopted from prior work, as a floor: treat simultaneous (A) untrusted input, (B) sensitive data and (C) state change or external communication as high-risk; an [A,B,C] agent needs per-action human approval, and [A,B] or [A,C] configurations need an explicit residual-risk assessment; the source notes the rule is silent on autonomy depth (p. 14) [BT].

5. <!-- concept: excessive-agency-complete-mediation --> **Excessive Agency, complete mediation and human confirmation.** "Excessive Agency is the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs from an LLM, regardless of what is causing the LLM to malfunction." [V] (LLM03, p. 23). Its root causes are excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy (p. 23) [AR]; sanitization "is not a root control for Excessive Agency" [V] (p. 23). Controls: minimal tools and functionality, no open-ended tools (run a shell command, fetch a URL) where a granular one will do, minimal permissions, tools run in the user's context, human approval for high-impact actions (pp. 24–25) [AP]; and complete mediation: "Implement authorization in logic rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed or not." [V] with a graduated policy (audit, warn, block, escalate) that lets reversible actions auto-approve and sends irreversible ones to a human (pp. 25–26) [AP]. Human confirmation must show the exact rendered action, not a summary; invisible characters can make the displayed action differ from the executed one, and "approval fatigue degrades reviewer judgment at volume" [V] (LLM01 #7, p. 14). Monitoring and rate limits with circuit breakers "will not prevent Excessive Agency but can limit the level of damage caused" [V] (p. 26).

6. <!-- concept: structural-output-validation --> **Structural validation in trusted code, not a second model call.** LLM01 control #2: define a strict output schema and validate every response in trusted application code before any downstream action, using structural validation rather than a second LLM call (p. 14) [AP]. Its stated limit: it catches format violations, not semantic manipulation; a schema-valid response can still carry a malicious SQL query or an exfiltration-formatted email body (p. 14) [AP]. LLM07 adds validating tool calls (arguments, authorization, preconditions, current state) before execution, and structured outputs with mandatory fields against omissions (p. 44) [AP].

7. <!-- concept: model-output-as-untrusted-input --> **Model output as input from any other user.** "Since LLM-generated content can be controlled by prompt input, this behavior is similar to providing users indirect access to additional functionality." [V] (LLM10, p. 55). The control: "Treat the model as any other user, adopting a zero-trust approach" [V] (p. 56). The sinks it names: a shell, exec or eval; HTML or Markdown in a browser; string-built SQL; file paths; email templates; terminals, logs and IDE panes that render control characters; and chat renderers that fetch images or link previews, an exfiltration channel (pp. 55–56) [AE]. Controls: encoding by destination, parameterized queries, control-character sanitization before interpreting sinks, and auto-rendering off by default (pp. 56–57) [AP]. The 2026 scope adds the insecure code assistants generate at scale (p. 7) [AP], and Scenario #6 is an application that compiles and deploys LLM-generated code without human review or security testing (p. 57) [AE].

8. <!-- concept: claim-check-act --> **Misinformation as a system failure: Claim-Check-Act.** Because model output now drives tool calls, code, inferred system state and authorizations, "This makes misinformation a system-level failure" [V] (LLM07, p. 43). "In agentic architectures, this overreliance is frequently embedded in system design." [V] (p. 43). Controls: ground claims in authoritative, current sources before acting; Claim-Check-Act patterns that separate generation from execution and verify claims before acting; verification signals, not just confidence; runtime verification for high-impact actions; log claims, evidence and outcomes (p. 44) [AP]. Common examples include incorrect state inference, where the model infers a condition has been met when it has not (p. 44) [AE]; Scenario #7 is fabricated task completion, an agent reporting a nightly backup that never ran (p. 45) [AE].

9. <!-- concept: hidden-context-is-discoverable --> **Hidden context is discoverable.** "Practitioners should design under the assumption that hidden context is discoverable and that any contents of the context should not be considered a secret." [V] (LLM08, p. 46). Hidden context covers the system prompt, developer instructions, retrieved policy text and tool schemas (p. 46) [AP]. No credentials, connection strings or tokens there, and no reliance on it as a boundary for authorization, privilege separation, policy enforcement or content filtering (p. 46) [AR]; "the real risk is that sensitive credentials are placed in the hidden context in the first place" [V] (pp. 47–48). Severity runs from informational to critical by what is placed there and how the application relies on it (p. 46) [AR]. Authorization is enforced deterministically and auditably outside the model (p. 48) [AP].

10. <!-- concept: model-and-tool-supply-chain --> **The model and tool supply chain.** Coding assistants hallucinate plausible package names, which attackers register in advance (*slopsquatting*), so an unverified AI-suggested dependency can resolve to malicious code (LLM04, p. 28) [BT]; verify that AI-suggested dependencies exist and are the intended package before adopting them (p. 30) [AP]. Artifacts resolved by a mutable reference (a latest tag) rather than an immutable digest can be swapped (p. 29) [AP]; a deleted or transferred namespace can be re-registered and pulled by name (Scenario #5, p. 31) [AE]. "Signing proves integrity and origin, not safety" [V] (p. 30) [AR]; "static analysis alone cannot establish behavioral safety" [V] (p. 29); scanners and safe-loader flags are defense-in-depth layers, not guarantees (p. 32) [AR]. LLM01 control #10 extends this to every MCP server and tool package: pin, sign, verify, audit tool descriptions for hidden instructions; pinning does not stop a payload in the pinned version (p. 15) [AP]. A build pipeline compromise passes the organization's own provenance checks because its own infrastructure signs the artifact (Scenario #7, p. 32) [AR].

11. <!-- concept: hard-caps-not-alerts --> **Hard caps, not alerts; agentic circuit breakers.** "A defining characteristic of this threat is cost asymmetry." [V] (LLM06, p. 38). Reasoning models, multimodal inputs and tool protocols that fan one request into many make it worse, and "Traditional request-rate limiting alone is no longer sufficient." [V] (p. 38). Controls: token- and cost-aware limits with pre-flight estimation; non-overridable spending caps that halt inference, "rather than alerting thresholds that fast-accumulating workloads can outpace" [V] (p. 40); step, recursion-depth and time limits and per-run cost ceilings on every agent execution, with state hashing to detect loops (p. 41) [AP]. A published malicious tool can drive an agent into recursive tool calls (Scenario #7, pp. 41–42) [AE]; the source warns of "hundreds of calls spawned from a single task" [V] (p. 39); a long agentic session's per-turn cost climbs from about $0.001 to about $0.50 by turn 100 with no single request tripping a rate limit (Scenario #8, p. 42) [AE].

12. <!-- concept: every-channel-is-an-output --> **Every channel is an output; memory writes are privileged.** Disclosure channels include tool-call arguments, reasoning traces, retrieved chunks, logs, telemetry, embeddings and observable inference properties, each to be treated as an output (LLM02, p. 18) [AR]: "Treat reasoning traces and tool arguments as outputs, not debugging leftovers." [V] (p. 19). For oversharing upstream, "The fix is the data surface, not the model" [V] (p. 18). "Cosine similarity does not respect ACLs." [V] Authorize before retrieval, because post-generation filtering cannot undo a chunk already given to the model (p. 19) [AR]; in LLM09, "A client-supplied scope is a suggestion, not a control." [V] (p. 52). Observability platforms log full prompts, completions and traces by default (p. 20) [AE], so logs and traces are scrubbed before monitoring ingestion (p. 20) [AP]. LLM01 control #9 treats agent memory writes as privileged: log the causing prompt, classify writes for instruction content, approve before instruction-bearing memories persist; incremental writes can evade per-write classification (pp. 14–15) [AP].

## Questions to Ask During Warranting Agent-Built Software

### Phase 1: Specifying the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Capability budget | Which of untrusted input, sensitive data, and state change or external communication will this feature (or the agent building it) hold at once? | LLM01 #8, p. 14 |
| Minimal agency | Which tools, functions and permissions does the task need, and which open-ended tools (shell, URL fetch) can be swapped for granular ones? | LLM03 #1–#4, pp. 24–25 |
| Human-gated actions | Which actions are high-impact or irreversible and need a human, and which are reversible enough to auto-approve? | LLM03 #6–#7, pp. 25–26 |
| Output contract | What schema must the model's output meet before anything downstream acts on it? | LLM01 #2, p. 14 |
| Spend ceiling | What hard cap halts this feature or agent run, per key, user and run? | LLM06 #2, #9, pp. 40–41 |
| What the agent decides alone | Which conditions will the model infer for itself (a check passed, an identity verified), and who checks them? | LLM07, pp. 43–44 |

### Phase 2: Triaging risk

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Route by shape | Does the feature read untrusted input (LLM01), touch sensitive data (LLM02), act through tools (LLM03), pull models or packages (LLM04), learn or store (LLM05, LLM09), spend (LLM06), drive decisions (LLM07), carry hidden instructions (LLM08) or feed a sink (LLM10)? | pp. 10–57 |
| Three legs | Does any agent in the change hold all three legs, and which leg can be removed? | LLM01, pp. 13–14 |
| Channels | Through which channels (answers, tool arguments, traces, logs, embeddings) could personal data leave? | LLM02, p. 18 |
| Retrieval authorization | Is access checked inside the index query, before the model sees a chunk, or filtered afterwards? | LLM02, p. 20; LLM09, p. 52 |
| Memory | Does the change write model output or user content into long-term memory or a retrieval corpus? | LLM01 #9, pp. 14–15 |
| Authorization path | Does anything rely on the model, or on a system prompt, to decide whether an action is allowed? | LLM03 #7, p. 25; LLM08, p. 48 |
| Reversibility | Which actions does the graduated policy auto-approve, and which escalate? | LLM03 #7, pp. 25–26 |

### Phase 3: Locking the tests

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Adaptive | Was the injection defense tested by someone who had read it, or only against a fixed attack set? | LLM01 #11, p. 15 |
| Indirect surfaces | Do the tests plant instructions in each surface the model reads (retrieved documents, tool output, memory, files), not only the user's input field? | LLM01, pp. 11–12 |
| Sinks | Is there a hostile payload test for each sink the output reaches (shell, SQL, path, HTML, terminal, renderer)? | LLM10, pp. 55–56 |
| State, not claims | Do the tests check the system's state after the action, or the model's account of it? | LLM07 #2, p. 44; Scenario #7, p. 45 |
| Backdoors | If a model or adapter was fine-tuned or replaced, were trigger-based probes run after alignment? | LLM05 #10, pp. 35–36 |
| Disclosure | For high-sensitivity data, is disclosure red-teaming a release gate? | LLM02 Tier 3, p. 21 |

### Phase 4: Building in the sandbox

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Untrusted reading | What untrusted or semi-trusted text (issues, tickets, READMEs, web pages, package metadata) does the coding agent read while holding tools? | LLM01, pp. 11–12, 16–17 |
| Credentials | Are credentials and state-change capability held in code behind a deterministic policy check, or handed to the agent? | LLM01 #4, p. 14 |
| Destructive commands | Does a human see the exact rendered command before anything destructive, external or irreversible runs? | LLM01 #7, p. 14 |
| Shell reach | Does the agent's shell, file-system or cloud-API access turn an injection into a host incident? | Scenario #8, p. 16 |
| Dependencies | Does each dependency the agent added exist, and is it the package intended? | LLM04 #2, p. 30 |
| Tools | Is every MCP server and tool package pinned, signed and its description read for hidden instructions? | LLM01 #10, p. 15 |
| Runaway | Do step, depth, time and cost limits stop the agent's run? | LLM06 #9, p. 41 |

### Phase 5: Gating deterministically

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Output sinks | Is every path from model output to a sink encoded for that sink or parameterized? | LLM10 #3–#5, #8–#9, pp. 56–57 |
| Validation | Is the output validated structurally in trusted code, and what semantic check covers what the schema cannot? | LLM01 #2, p. 14 |
| Invisible text | Are tag-block, variation-selector and zero-width characters stripped at ingest and render? | LLM01 #5, p. 14 |
| Secrets | Does any prompt template, system prompt or tool description hold a secret? | LLM08, p. 46 |
| References | Are models, adapters, datasets and tools resolved by immutable digest, not a name or a latest tag? | LLM04, p. 29 |
| Model artifacts | Are inference artifacts (chat templates, tokenizer configs, adapters) treated as code: signed, hash-checked, diffed? | LLM05 #12, p. 36 |
| Spend | Is the cost control a cap that halts, or an alert? | LLM06 #2, p. 40 |

### Phase 6: Reviewing independently

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Coverage | Did the review's injection analysis cover retrieved content, tool output and memory, or only the chat input? | LLM01, p. 12 |
| Where authorization lives | Did the reviewer find the deterministic check behind each privileged action? | LLM03 #7, pp. 25–26 |
| Stated limits | For each control the change relies on, did the review name its stated limit and the control that backs it? | LLM01, pp. 13–15 |
| Generated code | Is code the agent generated reviewed and security-tested before it is compiled and deployed? | LLM10 Scenario #6, p. 57 |

### Phase 7: Warranting the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Kinds of control | Which injection controls in the pack reduce success, and which bound the blast radius? Is there at least one of the second kind? | LLM01, p. 13 |
| Residual risk | For any two-leg configuration, is the residual-risk assessment on the pack? | LLM01 #8, p. 14 |
| Adaptive evidence | Does any attack-success figure in the pack come from adaptive testing? | LLM01 #11, p. 15 |
| Claims | Which completion claims were checked against state? | LLM07, pp. 44–45 |
| Signatures | Where the pack cites a signature, does it also cite a behavioural check? | LLM04 #5, p. 30 |
| Quiet record | Is a run of incident-free changes offered as evidence the controls can go? | p. 5 |

### Phase 8: Releasing and operating

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | Is cost attributed per key, user and session, with session-level growth watched? | LLM06, pp. 38, 42 |
| Tool use | Are tool calls and downstream actions logged and monitored? | LLM03 #8, p. 26 |
| Telemetry | Does the observability stack capture prompts, completions or traces by default, and are they scrubbed before export? | LLM02, p. 20 |
| Disclosure playbook | If data leaves through a model channel, is there a playbook to scope by data class and subject and clean up vectors, caches and memory? | LLM02 Tier 3, p. 21 |
| Embedding leaks | Would a leaked vector backup be treated as a leak of the documents behind it? | LLM09, pp. 51, 54 |

## What to Look For

| Signal | Diagnosis | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| The pack's only injection control is a filter, a classifier or a prompt rule | Controls of the kind expected to degrade against adaptive attackers; nothing bounds the blast radius (LLM01, p. 13) | Add a bounding control (least privilege, deterministic policy check, confirmed action) and state each control's limit |
| A block rate from a fixed attack set is quoted as evidence | A static-only claim the source says to reject (LLM01 #11, p. 15) | Require an adaptive run against the disclosed defense |
| The coding agent triages public issues with a full-rights database key | All three legs at once; trusted-backend indirect injection (Concept 4; Scenario #9, pp. 16–17) | Remove a leg: scoped read-only credentials, or no untrusted reading in that session |
| The agent's reply that the job is done is the evidence | Overreliance embedded in the harness; fabricated completion (LLM07, pp. 43, 45) | Check the state the claim names before anything acts on it |
| A second model call approves the first model's output | Validation by a second LLM call, which the source steers away from (LLM01 #2, p. 14) | Validate structurally in trusted code; add the semantic check the schema cannot make |
| Model output is concatenated into SQL, a shell line or HTML | Improper output handling at a named sink (LLM10, pp. 55–56) | Parameterize or encode for the sink; block until done |
| An API key sits in a system prompt or tool description | Secret in hidden context, which should be assumed discoverable (LLM08, p. 46) | Move it out of anything the model can reach |
| A model or MCP server is pulled by name or latest tag | Mutable reference; namespace reuse (LLM04, pp. 29, 31) | Pin by immutable digest |
| *Signed* is the whole supply-chain argument | Integrity and origin taken for safety (LLM04, p. 30) | Add a behavioural evaluation and provenance policy |
| The only spend control is an alert | Alerts that fast workloads can outpace (LLM06, p. 40) | A hard cap that halts, plus per-run agent limits |
| Reasoning traces or tool arguments go raw to a shared log | Channels not treated as outputs (LLM02, pp. 19–21) | Classify, redact and scrub before export |
| Human approval is a one-line summary clicked through dozens of times a day | The displayed action may differ from the executed one, and approval fatigue degrades judgment (LLM01 #7, p. 14) | Show the exact rendered action, and cut approvals to the irreversible ones |

## When to Use This Reference

Reach for this source when:

- A change adds or alters a model feature (an LLM call, prompt, tool, retrieval, memory, fine-tune or hosted model) and the builder needs its threat shape and named controls, with each control's limit.
- The coding agent reads text it did not write (issues, tickets, READMEs, web pages, package metadata) while holding tools or credentials.
- The pack must say which controls bound the damage when the model is fooled, rather than only lower the odds.
- Model output reaches a sink (shell, SQL, file path, HTML, email, terminal, renderer), a spend meter, or a log.
- The question is whether a signature, a scan, a block rate or a quiet record counts as evidence.

Reach elsewhere for agents that act with tools, memory and other agents in depth (`owasp-agentic-top10-2026`, `owasp-agentic-threats-mitigations`), for the development tasks and attestation that answer these threats (`nist-sp-800-218a`, `nist-ssdf-1-1`, `cisa-secure-software-attestation-form`), for verifiable application security requirements at a level (`owasp-asvs-5-0`), for the agent-harness controls of a vulnerability workflow (`openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai`), and for why models state guesses with confidence (`why-language-models-hallucinate-kalai`). This source is threat guidance ranked by vote and incident data; it does not measure whether its controls work.

## Worked Example

A two-person firm uses a coding agent to add an AI reply drafter to a client's support console. The drafter reads each ticket and the customer's order notes, drafts a reply, and can call a refund tool. The coding agent picks its tasks from the client's public issue tracker, opens pull requests, runs a shell, and has an MCP connection to a staging database holding a copy of production data, under a key with full rights. It reports the change done: tests green, refunds working. The builder starts the warranty pack.

**The agent first, then the feature.** The stance that shapes every step:

> "Build the system around it, so that when the model is fooled, and it will be, nothing important breaks." [V]

(p. 5; Concept 1). The reviewer agent runs the three-leg check on the coding agent itself (Concept 4). It reads public issues (untrusted input), reaches customer records (sensitive data), and can push code and run commands (state change). That is the source's trusted-backend case, where planted text in an issue or ticket is read by the developer's agent under elevated credentials:

> "The agent, not the attacker, performs the privileged action" [V]

(LLM01, p. 12; Scenario #9, pp. 16–17). The gate action: remove a leg. The staging copy of production data goes, the database key becomes read-only and scoped, and destructive or external commands need a human who sees the exact rendered command, with the source's warning about approval fatigue in mind (LLM01 #7, p. 14; Concept 5). This applies the source's application controls to the builder's own harness, which its developer-assistant scenarios support directly.

**Triage of the feature.** The drafter holds all three legs too: ticket text is untrusted (anyone can write a ticket), and the order notes sit on a trusted surface, the client's own database, which an attacker may still reach through an unrelated public form, customer data is sensitive, and the refund tool changes state (Concepts 3, 4). The agent's design lets the model decide whether a refund is allowed. The source is direct:

> "Implement authorization in logic rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed or not." [V]

(LLM03, p. 25). The builder adopts the source's own graduated example: a refund as store credit, which is recoverable, auto-approves; an external payout routes to a human (pp. 25–26; Concept 5). The refund tool takes arguments the model proposes, so they are validated in trusted code against a schema and then re-checked by the policy engine for amount and customer, since a schema catches format, not meaning (LLM01 #2, #4, p. 14; Concept 6).

**Gates.** The draft renders as Markdown in the agent console. The source names auto-rendered images and link previews as an exfiltration channel, so auto-rendering goes off and the draft is encoded for HTML (LLM10, pp. 55–57; Concept 7). Invisible Unicode is stripped where tickets come in and where drafts render (LLM01 #5, p. 14). The vendor model key was in the system prompt; it moves out, since hidden context should be assumed discoverable (LLM08, p. 46; Concept 9). The feature gets a hard spending cap per customer session, not an alert (LLM06, p. 40; Concept 11).

**Tests and the pack.** The agent's injection tests are fifteen fixed payloads typed into the ticket body. They pass. The pack's tests are widened to plant instructions in the order notes and in tool output, and a red-team run is made by someone given the defense, because a study the source cites

> "found static attack success near zero while adaptive attack success exceeded 90% for most of 12 recent defenses" [V]

(LLM01, p. 15; Concept 2). The agent's *refunds working* is checked against state: the test ledger shows the refund call was mocked and never reached the payments sandbox, the source's incorrect-state-inference failure in small (LLM07, pp. 44–45; Concept 8). The pack lists the controls in two columns, as the builder sorts them: those that lower injection odds (input filtering, prompt rules) and those that bound damage (scoped key, policy engine, payout approval, spend cap), each with its stated limit, so the accountable builder signs against the second column (LLM01, p. 13; Concept 2).

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

- **The unfoolable model.** Signal: the pack argues the prompt is robust. Diagnosis: the source says no reliable prevention mechanism exists today and defense is architectural (LLM01, p. 13). Follow-up: show what bounds the damage when the prompt fails.
- **Chat-box-only injection testing.** Signal: every injection test is typed into the user's input field. Diagnosis: indirect surfaces carry the high-impact cases, and chat-surface defenses miss them (LLM01, p. 12). Follow-up: plant instructions in each surface the model reads.
- **Static numbers as assurance.** Signal: a near-zero attack success rate from a fixed set. Diagnosis: static success near zero can sit beside adaptive success above 90% (LLM01, p. 15) [BT]. Follow-up: adaptive red-team with the defense disclosed.
- **The model as gatekeeper.** Signal: a prompt line saying *only admins may do X*. Diagnosis: authorization delegated to the model or to hidden context (LLM03, p. 25; LLM08, p. 48). Follow-up: move the check into deterministic code.
- **Model checks model.** Signal: a second LLM call approves output before a downstream action. Diagnosis: the source asks for structural validation in trusted code (LLM01 #2, p. 14). Follow-up: schema in code, plus a semantic check the schema cannot make.
- **The agent's word as state.** Signal: *done*, *backed up*, *refunded* taken from the agent's report. Diagnosis: incorrect state inference and fabricated completion (LLM07, pp. 44–45). Follow-up: Claim-Check-Act: check the state before acting on the claim.
- **Signed means safe.** Signal: a signature or a clean scan offered as proof of a model or package. Diagnosis: signing proves integrity and origin, not safety; scanners are layers, not guarantees (LLM04, pp. 30, 32). Follow-up: add behavioural evaluation and immutable references.
- **The alert as a cap.** Signal: spend is *monitored*. Diagnosis: alerts that fast workloads can outpace (LLM06, p. 40). Follow-up: a cap that halts and per-run agent limits.
- **Quiet months as proof.** Signal: *it's been fine for months*, offered to drop a control. Diagnosis: the source reads a low incident count as a defense effect (p. 5); carrying that to one team's history is a transfer. Follow-up: keep the bounding controls and build for the day the model is turned against you.

**Named tensions and disagreements.**

- *Safe serialisation: reduce, or eliminate.* `nist-sp-800-218a` (PW.6.1.C1) asks organisations to consider secure model serialisation mechanisms that reduce or eliminate vectors for introducing malicious content. This source says moving away from unsafe serialisation reduces but does not remove the risk: a backdoor can sit in the computational graph of a format widely considered safe, a crafted file can exploit the format's own parser, and scanners and safe-loader flags have had bypasses (LLM04, pp. 29, 32). For the warranty, a safe format is a layer; the pack still needs provenance and behavioural checks.
- *A second model as checker.* This source asks for structural validation in trusted code rather than a second LLM call before a downstream action (LLM01 #2, p. 14). `openssf-finding-fixing-vulnerabilities-ai` uses AI reviewers as a first pass on findings and fixes, while warning not to treat agreement among AI reviewers as proof and requiring empirical confirmation and human review of fixes. A tension in setting rather than a contradiction: this source speaks to a runtime gate on model output, the OpenSSF guide to development-time triage; both make the deciding check one that does not rest on a model's judgment.

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

**Borrowed-through gaps.** The source cites a large body of prior work: incident write-ups, vendor advisories and CVEs, academic attack papers, government security guidance, a companion OWASP data-security guide, and the nine external frameworks mapped in Appendix A. The three-leg pre-deployment check, the two-of-three capability floor and the adaptive-versus-static attack figure are each adopted from cited work [BT]; this distillation states them as the source uses them and does not name their originators. Of the works the source cites, only the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 (`owasp-agentic-top10-2026`) and OWASP ASVS (`owasp-asvs-5-0`, edition not named by the source) are held in this corpus. The LLM07 reference list names a 2025 work with the same title as `why-language-models-hallucinate-kalai`; the source does not cite it in the entry body, and the deep reference does not establish that the two are the same, so the integration row rests on the corpus's own deep reference, not on the citation. Incidents in the source's scenarios are described here without product names.

**Named limits of the source.** It owns the model as a component and defers agentic amplification (persistent memory, inter-agent channels, multi-step compromise) to the Agentic Top 10 (pp. 7, 47). It is a consensus ranking, three-quarters practitioner vote and a quarter incident data; the letter names neither the databases nor the classifiers, and gives the vote's size only as hundreds of practitioners (p. 5). Its controls carry stated limits and no measured effect sizes. The Appendix B architecture and threat-modeling content and Figures 1–3 are images the deep reference did not inspect (text-only scope), so nothing from them is used here. The document is dated August 2026 with placeholder publication dates in its front matter (pp. 1–2), a re-projection trigger when a final edition appears.

**Evidence-marker continuity.** Every quotation marked `[V]` is copied from a `[V]` passage in the deep reference, which passed Pass I on 2026-10-15. The four blockquotes in the worked example are `[V]` passages there; the adaptive-attack one is a fragment, introduced by the distillation's own words outside the quotation marks. Control-level paraphrases keep the deep reference's `[AP]`, the leads' and entries' framing keeps `[AR]`, common examples and scenarios keep `[AE]`, and points the source draws from cited work keep `[BT]`. The application of the defense-effect reading to one team's history, and of application controls to the coding agent's own sandbox beyond the source's developer-assistant scenarios, are marked as transfers.

## Runtime triggers this source addresses

| Trigger | Content from this source that addresses it | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|
| The builder says "the agent will figure out the details" | Overreliance embedded in system design; incorrect state inference; excessive autonomy as a root cause of Excessive Agency (LLM07, pp. 43–44; LLM03, p. 23) (Concepts 5, 8) | Name what the agent will decide alone and which of those decisions a check confirms; what it may do unchecked is its autonomy budget. |
| The diff touches login, sessions, tokens or permissions | Where a model or prompt sits on that path: authorization in deterministic logic, never the LLM; hidden context no security boundary; tools run in the user's context with minimum scope (LLM03 #5, #7, p. 25; LLM08, pp. 46, 48) (Concepts 5, 9) | If the model or a prompt decides who may do what, move that decision into code the model cannot talk past. |
| The change stores or moves personal data | Every channel an output; authorize before retrieval; minimize context; no secrets or regulated data in system prompts; scrub logs before monitoring ingestion (LLM02, pp. 18–20) (Concept 12) | List every channel the data can leave by, traces and logs included, and check access before retrieval, not after generation. |
| The change adds an LLM call, a prompt, a tool an agent can call, or memory | Route by the feature's shape across LLM01–LLM10; three-leg check and two-of-three floor; memory writes as privileged (pp. 10–57; LLM01, pp. 13–15) (Concepts 4, 12) | Name which of the three legs the feature holds, remove one if you can, and route it through the entries its shape touches. |
| A migration, a delete or a bulk update is in the plan | When a model or agent can trigger it: graduated enforcement, irreversible actions to human review; human confirmation of the exact rendered action (LLM03 #6–#7, pp. 25–26; LLM01 #7, p. 14) (Concept 5) | Irreversible means a human approves the exact command, not a summary of it. |
| A test checks the agent's output text rather than the system's state | Claim-Check-Act; incorrect state inference; fabricated task completion (LLM07, pp. 44–45) (Concept 8) | The agent's text is a claim; the test checks the state the claim names. |
| The suite passes, but nobody knows whether it would catch a wrong implementation | For injection defenses: static attack success near zero beside adaptive success above 90%; reject static-only claims (LLM01 #11, p. 15) [BT] (Concept 2) | A suite of known attacks shows only that known attacks fail; test it with someone who has read the defense. |
| "Skip permissions, it's been fine for months" | The defense effect; build for the day the model is turned against you; least privilege and capability budgets as load-bearing; an agent with shell, file-system or cloud-API access turns an injection into a host incident (pp. 5, 8; LLM01, pp. 13, 16) (Concepts 1, 2) | The quiet months are what the permissions bought. Keep them, because the surface the agent reads cannot be closed. |
| The agent's environment can reach production credentials or data | Credentials and state change held in code behind a deterministic policy engine, least privilege per operation; trusted-backend injection through a full-rights database connection (LLM01 #4, p. 14; Scenario #9, pp. 16–17; LLM03 #4, p. 25) (Concepts 3, 5) | Take the reach away, not just the intent: an agent that can read planted text and holds the key will use it for whoever planted it. |
| The agent reads untrusted content (web pages, issues, emails) while holding tools | Indirect injection on untrusted, semi-trusted and trusted surfaces; the three legs; provenance-labeled channels with their limit (LLM01, pp. 11–14) (Concepts 3, 4) | Reading and acting in one session with private data in reach is all three legs; split them or remove one. |
| The agent adds a dependency nobody asked for | Hallucinated package names registered in advance; verify AI-suggested dependencies exist and are intended; immutable digests (LLM04, pp. 28–30) [BT] (Concept 10) | Check the package is real, intended and pinned before it stays; a plausible name is what the attack relies on. |
| The agent runs for an hour unattended and reports success | Fabricated task completion; Claim-Check-Act; agentic circuit breakers with step, depth, time and cost limits (LLM07, pp. 44–45; LLM06 #9, p. 41) (Concepts 8, 11) | The report is a claim: check the state it names, and make sure the run had limits that would have stopped it. |
| The pack says "all tests pass" with no run record | Claim-Check-Act: separate the claim from the act and verify before acting; log claims, evidence and outcomes (LLM07, p. 44) (Concept 8) | No record, no check: send it back for the run. |
| The builder signs because the last ten went fine | Defense effect: a low incident count understates the risk the controls hold off (p. 5); controls that bound the blast radius survive adaptive attackers (LLM01, p. 13) (Concepts 1, 2) | Ten good changes say the controls worked, not that they can go; sign on the controls that bound the damage. |
| Something went wrong after release | Disclosure incident-response playbook: scope by data class and subject, notification duties, unlearning or withdrawal, vector and cache clean-up, persistent-memory audit; embedding leaks treated as document leaks (LLM02, p. 21; LLM09, pp. 53–54) (Concept 12) | If data may have left through a model channel, scope it by data class and clean the vectors, caches and memory, not just the code. |

| Trigger (proposed) | Phase | Content from this source | Teach-in-the-moment script |
|---|---|---|---|
| The story adds a model call, a tool or memory and states no capability budget, output schema or spend cap | Phase 1 | Two-of-three floor (LLM01 #8, p. 14); strict output schema (LLM01 #2, p. 14); hard spending caps (LLM06 #2, p. 40) | Write the three legs it holds, the schema its output must meet, and the cap that halts it, before the build. |
| The change writes model output or user content into an agent's long-term memory or a retrieval corpus | Phase 2 | Memory writes as privileged: log the causing prompt, classify for instruction content, approve before instruction-bearing entries persist (LLM01 #9, pp. 14–15) | Treat a memory write like a privileged action: logged, classified and approved. |
| Retrieval filters by tenant or permission after the search, or trusts a scope the client sends | Phase 2 | "Cosine similarity does not respect ACLs." [V] (LLM02, p. 19); "A client-supplied scope is a suggestion, not a control." [V] (LLM09, p. 52) | Put the access check inside the index query, on the server. |
| An LLM feature's injection tests cover only the user's input field | Phase 3 | Indirect surfaces; chat-surface-only defenses miss them (LLM01, pp. 11–12) | Plant instructions in every surface the model reads. |
| The coding agent is about to run a destructive or irreversible command (a delete, a force push, a cloud-API teardown) | Phase 4 | Human confirmation of the exact rendered action, with its limits (LLM01 #7, p. 14); shell, file-system or cloud-API access amplifies an injection into a host incident (Scenario #8, p. 16) | A human sees the exact command before it runs. |
| The agent installs or enables an MCP server, skill or tool package, or edits a tool definition or MCP configuration | Phase 4 | Pin, sign and verify every MCP server and tool package; audit tool descriptions for hidden instructions; pinning does not stop a payload in the pinned version (LLM01 #10, p. 15); a published malicious tool can drive an agent into recursive loops (LLM06 Scenario #7, pp. 41–42) | Read the tool's description for instructions, pin and verify it, and cap the runs it can trigger. |
| Model or agent output reaches exec, eval, a shell, string-built SQL, a file path, HTML, an email template, a terminal or an auto-rendering chat UI | Phase 5 | Zero-trust treatment of output; encoding by destination; parameterized queries; control-character sanitization; auto-render off (LLM10, pp. 55–57) | Block until the output is encoded for that sink or parameterized. |
| A model's output is checked by a second model call before a downstream action | Phase 5 | Structural validation in trusted code rather than a second LLM call; a schema catches format, not semantics (LLM01 #2, p. 14) | Validate in code, then add the semantic check a schema cannot make. |
| A secret, key, token or connection string appears in a system prompt, prompt template or tool description | Phase 5 | Hidden context is discoverable; no credentials in it (LLM08, pp. 46–48) | Move it to something the model cannot reach. |
| A model, adapter, dataset, tool or MCP server is referenced by name, tag or *latest* with no digest | Phase 5 | Mutable references and re-registered namespaces let artifacts be swapped (LLM04, pp. 29, 31); inference artifacts treated as code (LLM05 #12, p. 36) | Pin by immutable digest. |
| The only cost control on a model call or agent loop is an alert or a requests-per-second limit | Phase 5 | "Traditional request-rate limiting alone is no longer sufficient." [V] (LLM06, p. 38); hard caps and agentic circuit breakers (pp. 40–41) | Add a cap that halts and per-run agent limits. |
| Text from tickets, files or web pages reaches the model or a renderer without invisible characters stripped | Phase 5 | Strip tag-block, variation-selector and zero-width characters at every ingest and render boundary; it does not stop visible payloads (LLM01 #5, p. 14) | Strip invisible characters on the way in and on the way out. |
| A review's injection analysis covers only the chat input | Phase 6 | "Defenses that focus only on the chat surface miss this entirely." [V] (LLM01, p. 12) | Extend the review to retrieved content, tool output and memory. |
| The agent's generated code is compiled and deployed with no human review or security testing | Phase 6 | LLM10 Scenario #6 (p. 57); the 2026 scope includes insecure code assistants generate (p. 7) | Treat the agent's code as model output: review and security-test it before it ships. |
| The pack quotes a block rate from a fixed attack set, or lists a filter or prompt rule as the only injection control | Phase 7 | Reject static-only claims; two kinds of control (LLM01, pp. 13, 15) | Require an adaptive run and at least one control that bounds what a fooled model can reach. |
| A signature or a clean scan is the pack's evidence that a model or package is safe | Phase 7 | "Signing proves integrity and origin, not safety" [V] (LLM04, p. 30); scanners are layers, not guarantees (p. 32) | A signature says who and what, not whether it is safe; add a behavioural check. |
| An agent holds two of the three legs and the pack carries no residual-risk assessment | Phase 7 | [A,B] or [A,C] configurations need an explicit residual-risk assessment (LLM01 #8, p. 14) | Write the residual risk of the two legs it holds. |
| An observability or tracing SDK ships with default capture of prompts, completions or traces | Phase 8 | These platforms log full prompts, completions, chunks and traces by default; scrub before monitoring ingestion (LLM02, p. 20) | Scrub before export, or turn the capture off. |
| Model spend climbs release after release, or long sessions grow in cost | Phase 8 | Cost attribution and session-level growth; per-turn cost climbing with context (LLM06, pp. 38, 42) | Attribute cost per key, user and session, and cap the session. |
| A leaked vector store or embedding backup is classed low severity because *only embeddings leaked* | Phase 8 | Embeddings can be inverted; treat such leaks as source-document leaks (LLM02, p. 19; LLM09, pp. 51, 54) | Treat it as a leak of the documents behind it. |
